title: Outcome harvesting
container: Ford Foundation, Middle East and North Africa Office, Cairo. May 2012, revised November 2013
note: Start here. The 27-page brief that set out the method: the definition of an outcome (p. 2), the four roles in a harvest (p. 4) and the six steps, one section each from p. 6. This repo cites the November 2013 revision; see errata.

title: Outcome harvesting: Principles, steps, and evaluation applications
container: Information Age Publishing, Charlotte, NC. Evaluation and Society series
note: The full statement of the method. Defines an outcome as an observable change in behaviour (p. 1), gives a chapter to each of the six steps (pp. 29 to 147) and sets out five process principles (pp. 149 to 167) and four content principles (pp. 169 to 187). Copyright 2019; released November 2018. Not open access.

authors: Wilson-Grau, R. and Kosterink, P. and Scheers, G.
title: Outcome Harvesting: A developmental evaluation inquiry framework supporting the development of an international social change network
container: Developmental evaluation exemplars: Principles in practice (M. Q. Patton, K. McKegg and N. Wehipeihana, Eds.), Guilford Press
note: OH used as the inquiry framework in a developmental evaluation of a global peacebuilding network.

authors: Wilson-Grau, R. and Britt, H. and Dewata, Y. and Rogers, P. and Stevens, K.
title: Outcome harvesting
container: BetterEvaluation, approach page. Original author R. Wilson-Grau; revised by H. Britt, Y. Dewata, P. Rogers and K. Stevens. Last updated 27 June 2024
note: Free overview of the six steps and the nine principles, with links to guides and examples. Its principle names follow Chapter 1 of the book, except one; see errata.

title: Outcome-based learning field guide: Tools to harvest and monitor outcomes and systematically learn from complex projects
container: World Bank, Washington, DC. Working Paper 90176
note: Practical tools built from pilots with World Bank teams. Its outcome definition is narrower than the brief: a change in the people, groups, communities or organisations a programme works with directly (p. 9). Open access.

title: Outcome harvesting
note: Five-page summary of the steps with a plain list of strengths and weaknesses (p. 3 onwards). Free.

title: The use of Outcome Harvesting in learning-oriented and collaborative inquiry approaches to evaluation: An example from Calgary, Alberta
note: OH used as a shared learning process across neighbourhood community development projects in Calgary, from 2013, with lessons for others adopting it (p. 47).

authors: Beardmore, A. and Jones, M. and Seal, J.
title: Outcome harvesting as a methodology for the retrospective evaluation of small-scale community development interventions
note: Tests OH on a place-based community wellbeing project. Finds it promising, with two limits: reaching a broad range of participants, and finding enough time and resources (p. 1). Open access, CC BY 4.0.

title: A family resemblance: Outcome Harvesting and QuIP compared
container: Bath Social and Development Research, blog post, 4 July 2017
note: Short comparison of OH with the Qualitative Impact Protocol, from the QuIP side.

title: Cases in outcome harvesting: Ten pilot experiences identify new learning from multi-stakeholder projects to improve results
container: World Bank, Washington, DC. Working Paper 90172
note: Ten pilot harvests in World Bank projects, among them pharmaceutical procurement in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda (p. 6). Open access.

authors: Smith, R. and Scheers, G. and Robinson, G.
title: Outcome harvesting evaluation of 20 years of cooperation between the Danish and Ugandan Disability Movements, 1996-2018
container: Disabled Peoples Organisations Denmark (DPOD). Final report, November 2020
note: A full harvest from Uganda, from design to outcome database, with its adaptation of the six steps and its substantiation responses in annexes (p. 3).

authors: Tomei, G. and Terenzi, L. and Testi, E.
title: Using Outcome Harvesting to evaluate socio-economic development and social innovation generated by Social Enterprises in complex areas. The case of BADAEL project in Lebanon
note: OH used to evaluate social enterprise development in Lebanon. Details confirmed on the journal and RePEc records; not yet read for this course.

title: Use of Outcome Harvesting for monitoring and evaluation: Our experiences and lessons learned
note: Lessons from using OH to monitor the Dialogue and Dissent programme in East Africa.

authors: Rassmann, K. and Smith, R. and Mauremootoo, J. and Wilson-Grau, R.
title: Retrospective 'outcome harvesting': Generating robust insights
note: OH used at the end of a global voluntary network programme, BioNET, 2007 to 2011.

title: 52 weeks of BetterEvaluation: Week 16: Identifying and documenting emergent outcomes of a global network
note: The blog that introduces the BioNET harvest paper: why a logframe did not fit a global network, and what the harvest found.

authors: Earl, S. and Carden, F. and Smutylo, T.
title: Outcome mapping: Building learning and reflection into development programs
note: Where the OH definition of an outcome comes from, as the brief records (Wilson-Grau and Britt 2013, p. 1). Open access.

title: The 'Most Significant Change' (MSC) technique: A guide to its use
note: The standard guide to MSC, the other approach that collects stories of change without fixing indicators in advance. Free.

authors: Copestake, J. and Morsink, M. and Remnant, F.
title: Attributing development impact: The Qualitative Impact Protocol case book
note: Cases using QuIP, which asks intended beneficiaries about change without naming the intervention. Read beside Copestake (2017). Open access.

title: Revisiting contribution analysis
note: The current statement of contribution analysis, the method this course pairs with OH: harvest the outcomes, then test the important ones.

title: Discussion note: Complexity-aware monitoring
container: USAID, Monitoring and Evaluation Series, Version 2.0, December 2013
note: Places OH among five complexity-aware monitoring approaches (p. 7) and explains why such methods look for unintended as well as intended results (p. 11).
